title: The digestive system and metabolism
note: Digestion breaks food into absorbable units: starch into monosaccharides, proteins into amino acids, and triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides. Most digestion and absorption happen in the small intestine, driven by pancreatic enzymes and bile. Cells then oxidize glucose through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain.

read.title: The long road of a fat molecule
text: Fat is the hardest nutrient to digest because it does not mix with water. Lipases in the mouth and stomach begin the work, but nearly all fat digestion happens in the small intestine.

When fatty chyme enters the duodenum, the intestinal wall releases cholecystokinin (CCK). CCK prompts the pancreas to secrete enzyme-rich juice and sends bile, made by the liver and concentrated in the gallbladder, into the duodenum. Bile salts act like a detergent: they break large fat globules into tiny droplets. This emulsification splits no molecules, but it greatly increases the surface area that pancreatic lipase can attack. Lipase then cleaves triglycerides into free fatty acids and monoglycerides.

These products ride to the brush border inside micelles, tiny clusters of bile salts whose water-friendly surfaces let them move through watery chyme. The lipids slip into the absorptive cells, where they are rebuilt into triglycerides and packaged with protein into chylomicrons.

Chylomicrons are too large to enter blood capillaries. Instead they pass into the lacteal at the center of each villus, travel through lymphatic vessels, and reach the blood through the thoracic duct. Sugars and amino acids take a different route: they enter blood capillaries and travel first to the liver through the hepatic portal vein.
